modalities.name: Keep the Garden Lit
modalities.tagline: Dance hard enough, in the right places, to keep every lamp on.
modalities.whatItIs: A self-run evening dance in a garden or yard at dusk, set around four to six motion-sensor lamps that switch off after about half a minute without movement, so the group has to keep spreading out and dancing near every lamp to keep the whole garden lit. Everything in it is outside you and happening now, real lights, real friends and eyes wide open with nobody in charge, which puts it at the far end from the eyes-closed, therapist-led imagined caring figures of the Ideal Parent Figure protocol.
modalities.coreIdea: Watching for the lamp that is about to go dark, and for who is already heading to it, is meant to keep attention on the space and the people in it, with nothing pictured or remembered. A shared, visible job with no winner is meant to turn a party into a playful bit of teamwork.
modalities.whatYouDo: Four to twelve friends set the lamps out across a garden or yard, hang a string of dim lights around the edge so it is never fully dark, warm up together over the first few songs, then dance hard in rounds of three songs for about an hour, moving between lamps as they fade and calling out when one goes dark. Between rounds the lamps are moved to new spots, and the last round is danced with every lamp set to stay on, so people can finally dance wherever they like.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who spend a lot of time in their heads at parties and want a silly, outward reason to keep moving with friends. It may suit groups who like to dance together without a teacher.
modalities.cautions: Dancing in half-light brings trips and bumps, so keep the dim edge lights on, clear the lawn of toys, hoses and holes, use battery lamps with no trailing cables, warm up, check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems and stop at once for chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Keep the music and lights considerate of neighbors, and any partner dancing or touch happens only when both people agree.
modalities.tweet: Untested idea for dusk: a garden of motion-sensor lamps that switch off after half a minute of stillness, so your friends have to keep dancing near every one to keep the whole place lit. No teacher, no winner. Keep a dim light on, clear the lawn.

modalities.name: Answer Across the Lawn
modalities.tagline: Small dance groups across a park answer each other in opposites.
modalities.whatItIs: A self-run outdoor dance in which small clusters of friends spread across a park lawn in facing pairs and keep answering each other by sight: when the cluster opposite goes high, yours goes low, when they speed up, you slow down, when they spread out, you bunch together. Everything that matters is out in plain view, groups of real bodies across the grass, which turns the inner cast of Internal Family Systems, many parts inside one person explored with a therapist, inside out. Nobody leads and nothing is explained.
modalities.coreIdea: Never copying, always answering, means you have to keep reading another group at a distance and work out what its opposite would be. A park full of contrasting shapes, each one made because of another, may make a scattered crowd feel joined up without anyone in charge.
modalities.whatYouDo: Twelve to forty people meet on a flat, open lawn on a dry day, warm up together for ten minutes and split into clusters of three to five, each facing a partner cluster about 15 meters away, around one speaker playing upbeat music. For about 45 minutes each cluster dances hard while answering its partner in opposites (high or low, fast or slow, wide or tight, travelling or on the spot), the pairings change every three songs so each cluster faces a new one, and the session ends with everyone walking in to dance one song together in the middle.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find inner exploration tiring and would rather spend an evening watching and answering what others are doing. It may suit groups who like open spaces and playful rules more than steps to learn.
modalities.cautions: Answering a fast group by going very low or very wide can strain knees and backs, so take only what your joints allow, keep jumps optional, check the grass for holes, wet patches and slopes, warm up, check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems and stop for chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Bring water and sun protection, keep the volume considerate of others in the park, and agree on any touch within a cluster before it happens.
modalities.tweet: An idea for a summer evening: small dance groups spread across a park, each facing another, and answer in opposites. They spread out, you bunch up; they speed up, you slow down. No leader, no steps to learn. Warm up, and mind holes in the grass.

modalities.name: Busker Crawl
modalities.tagline: Friends wander town and dance to whichever street musicians they find.
modalities.whatItIs: A self-run outing in which a small group of friends walks through a busy town center on a weekend afternoon and dances to every street musician they come across, whatever they happen to be playing. There is no plan, no route and no way to choose the music, about as far from CBT's agendas, records and tested predictions as dancing can get.
modalities.coreIdea: When you cannot pick or predict the next sound, there is nothing to get right, only something to meet as it arrives. Doing that together, out in a real street full of sound and people, is meant to make an unplanned moment feel like an invitation rather than a problem.
modalities.whatYouDo: Three to eight friends warm up at a meeting point, then wander for about 90 minutes, and at each of the five to eight buskers they find, whether a violinist, a steel pan player or a teenager with a guitar, they ask with a nod or a word whether they may dance, then dance hard for two or three songs before leaving a tip and moving on. Between stops they walk briskly, and the afternoon ends wherever the last busker is, with no rating or ranking of who was best.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like to plan everything and want a playful taste of moving with what they could not choose. It may suit friends who enjoy town centers and live music but rarely stop to join in.
modalities.cautions: Ask each musician first, leave a tip, keep out of doorways and walkways, agree on any partner holds within the group, and watch for uneven paving, traffic, crowds and wet surfaces. Warm up, carry water, check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems and stop at once for chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness.
modalities.tweet: Proposed: a busker crawl. A few friends wander town, and at every street musician they find (violin, steel pan, a kid with a guitar) they ask, dance hard for a couple of songs, tip and move on. No plan, no playlist. Ask first, and mind the paving.

modalities.name: Dancing to One Heart
modalities.tagline: A group dances to one member's heartbeat, played aloud through a speaker.
modalities.whatItIs: A small-group dance in which, for the main dance, the only beat in the room is one dancer's own heart, picked up by a chest-strap monitor and played through a speaker as a soft drum, so the tempo rises as everyone dances harder and falls as the pacer eases off. ACT leans on words, metaphors and talk about values, while here everything is felt and heard instead, using the plainest bodily signal there is, shared out loud.
modalities.coreIdea: Moving to a beat made by a real body ties the group to one person's effort, breath and limits in a way nobody has to describe. The pace has no plan, only a body to follow, which is meant to make keeping time with others something you do rather than think about.
modalities.whatYouDo: After learning the setup from a teacher in a first session, six to fifteen people meet in a hall, warm up to a recorded track, then dance hard for about 45 minutes to the live heartbeat of a volunteer pacer, adding claps and stamps on the beat, with a new pacer about every eight minutes. The pacer dances along, and when their heart rate passes a ceiling agreed in advance, well below their maximum, they sit down, so the beat slows and the whole room slows with it.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are tired of talking about how they feel and want a lively, wordless way to move with others. It may suit groups curious about how one person's body can set the pace for a room.
modalities.cautions: Everyone with heart, lung or joint problems checks with a doctor before joining, and only people with a doctor's clear go-ahead act as pacer; the ceiling is set low, the pacer sits as soon as it is reached, and everyone warms up, may dance at half time, agrees before any partner touch and stops at once for chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. The heartbeat belongs to the pacer, is never recorded or shared, and nobody is pushed to volunteer.
modalities.tweet: What if the only beat in the room were someone's heart? Concept: a chest monitor plays one dancer's heartbeat through a speaker and the group dances to it, faster as everyone works harder. Doctor check first, warm up, and the pacer sits at a low ceiling.

modalities.name: Kicking Through the Pile
modalities.tagline: Friends rake one huge leaf pile, then dance through it to music.
modalities.whatItIs: A self-run autumn outing in which friends rake fallen leaves into one big pile in a garden, or in a park where raking is allowed, then dance through it to loud music, kicking, scooping and throwing leaves as they go. Nothing in it means anything beyond crunch, smell and the drift of leaves through the air.
modalities.coreIdea: There is no hidden emotional sense to uncover, of the kind Coherence Therapy looks for with a therapist, only sound, texture and effort. Pure sensation shared with friends is meant to offer a rest from looking for reasons.
modalities.whatYouDo: Four to fifteen people spend 15 minutes raking together as a warm-up and check the pile for sticks and stones, then dance through it for 30 to 40 minutes to fast songs on a speaker, breathing hard, re-raking between songs and taking turns to toss armfuls into the air. The session ends with the leaves raked back where they belong, bagged or spread over flower beds, and nobody asks what any of it meant.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who have spent a lot of time searching for reasons and would like an afternoon where nothing needs interpreting. It may suit anyone who misses rough, noisy outdoor play.
modalities.cautions: Check the leaves for sticks, stones, glass, dog mess and wasps, wear gloves to rake, avoid leaves near roads, watch for slippery wet patches and never throw leaves at anyone's face; people with mold or pollen allergies or asthma may prefer to sit this out. Warm up, check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems and stop at once for chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness.
modalities.tweet: Idea for autumn: rake one huge leaf pile with friends, put on fast music and dance through it, kicking and tossing leaves, then rake it all back. Nothing to interpret, just crunch and noise. Check the pile for sticks, glass and dog mess first.

modalities.name: Told, Then Danced
modalities.tagline: One teammate describes a hidden dance clip; two others dance it.
modalities.whatItIs: A lively team game, learned from a teacher, in which one person watches a short dance clip the others cannot see and describes it in words alone, while two teammates try to dance it from the description. Then the clip is shown and everyone sees how close they came. It is the reverse of TRE's quiet, wordless shaking, done alone and left to happen by itself: deliberate moves built from someone else's words, in a noisy room full of people.
modalities.coreIdea: Turning words into movement asks dancers to listen hard, choose quickly and fit their bodies to another person's picture, so every move is intended and shared. The gap between what was said and what was danced is usually funny, and laughing at it together is meant to make getting things wrong feel light.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a warm-up, 12 to 30 people split into teams of three, and in each round the describer watches a 20 to 30 second clip on a phone, such as a folk dance, a music video or an old film musical, and has two minutes to talk the dancers through it without demonstrating. The dancers try the moves as they listen, perform the result to the music three times at full size and then watch the clip with everyone, roles rotate, and every few rounds the whole room dances all the clips learned so far, for about an hour in all.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want lively, chatty contact with a group and enjoy a game that mixes talking, thinking and moving. It may also suit anyone who laughs easily at their own mistakes, or would like to.
modalities.cautions: Describers skip flips, lifts, drops and anything else risky, dancers keep to what their joints allow, any partner hold in a clip is tried only if both dancers agree, and the floor stays clear and non-slip. Check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems, warm up, and stop for chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness.
modalities.tweet: New game for a dance class: one teammate watches a short clip you can't see and describes it in words only, no demonstrating, while you and a partner dance what you hear. Then everyone watches the clip and laughs. Describers skip the flips.

modalities.name: Through the Moving Gates
modalities.tagline: Dance through drifting foam gates, choosing over, under or around.
modalities.whatItIs: A teacher-run game in which a third of the room holds long foam pool noodles as gates that slowly rise, fall and drift, and everyone else dances through them on the beat, deciding in an instant whether to step over, duck under or go around each one. Roles rotate every song.
modalities.coreIdea: With a gate coming toward you there is no time to wait for anything to become clear, as Focusing patiently does, only to pick a way through and commit to it with the whole body. Practicing quick, whole-body choices in a silly game is meant to make deciding feel lighter.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a warm-up, 12 to 30 people in a sports hall take turns as gate holders, a third at a time in pairs, each pair holding one noodle between them and dancing on the spot as they slowly change its height and angle, while everyone else travels through the field of gates without stopping for the length of a song. The teacher speeds up the music and the gates as the session goes on, and after about 40 minutes everyone finishes with one slow song danced through gates held still.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who tend to deliberate and hesitate and would like a playful place to practice choosing fast. It may suit anyone who loved playground games and misses moving around with others.
modalities.cautions: Use soft foam only, keep gates between knee and chest height and never swing them, make ducking a bend of the knees rather than a dive, and slow the tempo when the room is crowded. Warm up, use a clear, non-slip floor, check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems and stop at once for chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness.
modalities.tweet: Suppose a third of a sports hall held foam pool noodles as gates that slowly rise, fall and drift, and everyone else danced through on the beat, choosing in a split second: over, under or around. Then you swap. Soft foam only, no swinging.

modalities.name: Step List Season
modalities.tagline: Friends write a list of dance moves and master them together.
modalities.whatItIs: A self-run, goal-driven dance practice in which a small group of friends writes a list of moves they want to master, then drills them together until each one is ticked off. Its pull is toward deliberate change and measured progress with no coach at all, the reverse of Aletheia coaching's gentle, coach-led uncovering of what is already true.
modalities.coreIdea: A concrete list and a visible tick give effort a clear direction, and learning with friends adds accountability without a teacher. The point is the plain pleasure of getting better at something on purpose.
modalities.whatYouDo: Three to six friends agree on ten to fifteen moves from videos, such as a spin, a footwork pattern or a basic partner turn, and meet twice a week for an hour in a room or garage. Each session starts with a warm-up and a run-through of mastered moves, then drills one new move until everyone has filmed a clean version, and the season ends with a party where the whole list is danced to a favorite song.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like goals and visible progress and want a sociable, sweaty skill to aim them at. It may suit those who find open-ended reflection frustrating and prefer to learn by doing.
modalities.cautions: Moves copied from videos can be beyond your current strength or flexibility, so learn them slowly, skip lifts, flips and drops, warm up, check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems and stop for pain, chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Film only people who agree to it, agree before any partner hold, and keep the floor clear and non-slip.
modalities.tweet: An idea: grab a few friends, write a list of 12 dance moves you've always wanted to nail, and meet twice a week until each one is ticked off. No coach, just a list, a phone camera and a party at the end. Learn slowly and skip the flips.

modalities.name: Never Drop the Dance
modalities.tagline: Teams keep one vigorous routine going by handing it on mid-move.
modalities.whatItIs: A taught group class in which teams of six turn one lively routine into a relay: each dancer performs a short, hard section and hands it to the next on the exact count, while the rest keep a driving step going behind, so the dance never stops for a whole song. Every handoff takes effort, timing and attention from everyone, which puts it about as far from Do Nothing meditation's dropping of all effort and aim as dance can go.
modalities.coreIdea: Carrying the thread for your team, then picking it up again a few seconds later, asks for steady effort and attention every minute. A visible shared goal, one song with no break in it, is meant to give that effort a clear purpose.
modalities.whatYouDo: A teacher warms up 18 to 40 people, teaches a 48-count routine of travelling steps, turns, claps and an optional jump, and splits it into six eight-count sections, one per team member, each of whom must start exactly as the dancer before lands their last count while the others keep a step-and-clap going in a line behind. Over 75 minutes teams practice their handoffs, then run the routine on a loop through faster and faster songs, aiming for one full song without a dropped count, and the session ends with all teams dancing the whole routine together.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel adrift or unmotivated and want a clear, shared challenge that asks something of them every minute. It may suit those who enjoy teamwork, timing and the moment a run finally comes together.
modalities.cautions: The routine is danced many times at full energy, so check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems, never skip the warm-up, keep jumps optional and stop at once for chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Teams need room to travel without colliding, the teacher offers a simpler version of every section, and a dropped count is laughed off, never blamed on anyone.
modalities.tweet: About as far from doing nothing as dance gets: a concept where teams of six keep one lively routine going as a relay, each dancer taking an eight-count section and handing it on exactly on the beat while the rest keep stepping. Goal: a whole song, no drop.

modalities.name: Whoever Is Near
modalities.tagline: An open-air dance where your partner is always whoever is nearest.
modalities.whatItIs: A monthly open-air dance in a town square, a park bandstand or a car-free street, open to anyone passing by, with one rule: you are always dancing with someone, and that someone is whoever happens to be next to you, for as long as you stay near each other. Partners change as the crowd drifts, regulars and newcomers mix, and nobody chooses.
modalities.coreIdea: Unlike metta's set order of chosen people held in mind with repeated wishes, there is no choosing, no phrases and no feeling to produce, only the actual person beside you, a friend or a stranger, for as long as you stay close. Meeting each one with plain attention to how they move may feel like a simple, physical kind of company.
modalities.whatYouDo: A volunteer teacher sets up a speaker, leads a ten-minute warm-up for whoever has gathered, explains the rule on a sign and by example, then plays upbeat music for about an hour while 15 to 60 people dance facing, answering or loosely matching whoever is nearest and drifting on whenever either moves away. Newcomers can join at any point, and the hour ends with one slow song danced by everyone in one loose crowd.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who tend to stick with the same few friends and would like an easy way to dance with many different people, including neighbors they have never met. It may suit anyone curious about others but put off by forced warmth or sharing circles.
modalities.cautions: Outdoor floors bring trips and bumps, so choose flat, dry paving clear of traffic, keep speeds moderate, warm up, check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems and stop for chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Touch happens only when both people nod, a clear step back always ends a pairing, the teacher watches for anyone who seems uncomfortable, and anyone can rest at the edge.
modalities.tweet: One untested rule for an open-air dance in a town square: you're never dancing alone, and your partner is always whoever is nearest, regular or passer-by. No choosing, just meet the next person and drift on. Touch only when both nod.

modalities.name: Talk and Twirl Nights
modalities.tagline: A dance night where chatting while you dance is the point.
modalities.whatItIs: A fast, energetic dance night in a hall or a bar with a big floor and the music kept low enough to talk, where small groups dance and chat at the same time, about anything at all. Attention keeps moving between the music, your feet, the people around you and what they are saying, the opposite of jhana's silent, solitary absorption in a single object.
modalities.coreIdea: Moving, listening and talking at once is meant to keep attention loose, quick and social instead of narrow and deep. Shared laughter on a busy floor is meant to bring a lightness that does not depend on concentration.
modalities.whatYouDo: A host sets the music at a volume where people can hear each other, warms everyone up, then lets 15 to 40 people dance in twos, threes and fours for about 90 minutes, talking as they move and drifting between groups. Songs are fast and the dancing is hard, about the effort of a steady run, where you can still get out a short sentence but not much more, so talk comes in quick bursts, jokes and questions answered on the next turn, and a few slower songs give people a chance to catch their breath.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who love both dancing and talking but find most dance floors too loud for one and most parties too still for the other. It may suit anyone who finds that focused practices leave them tense.
modalities.cautions: Talking while dancing hard can leave you short of breath, so if you cannot get a short sentence out, ease off, warm up, check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems and stop at once for chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Partner holds and spins happen only when both people agree, either can end one at any time, and the floor stays clear with the music moderate to protect hearing and voices.
modalities.tweet: Most dance floors are too loud to talk on. A concept: fast, sweaty dance nights with the music turned down so small groups can dance and chat at once. You should still be able to get out a short sentence, and if you can't, ease off.

modalities.name: Feet Choose the Song
modalities.tagline: Two songs play at opposite ends; the emptier end fades out.
modalities.whatItIs: An open dance night in which two different songs start at once from speakers at opposite ends of a hall, and the crowd decides which one survives simply by dancing toward it: after a minute the emptier end fades out and the whole room joins the other. Then two new songs start, and the room moves again.
modalities.coreIdea: Vipassana watches experience come and go, silently and alone, without trying to change it; here a crowd changes its own state out loud and together, one song at a time, using nothing but where it dances. Watching the room tip toward the song you picked, or choosing to follow it, may make shaping a shared mood feel possible.
modalities.whatYouDo: A host warms up 15 to 40 people, then runs pairs of mostly upbeat songs for about an hour, often contrasting ones such as a samba against a rock song or a waltz against a drum track, and after about a minute fades out the side with fewer dancers. Anyone can rest at a side wall, and for the last pair the host lets both songs play to the end so people can dance to whichever they like.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel stuck in a flat mood and want a playful, low-key way to try changing it with others. It may also suit shy people who would like their choices to count in a group without having to speak.
modalities.cautions: Crossing the hall in a crowd can cause collisions, so walk rather than run to the side you choose, keep the floor clear and non-slip, warm up, check with a doctor first if you have heart, lung or joint problems and stop at once for chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Keep both speakers at moderate volume, and anyone who finds the shifting, crowded room too much can rest at the side wall.
modalities.tweet: Can a dance floor choose its own mood? Here's an idea: two songs start at once from opposite ends of a hall, everyone dances toward the one they want, and after a minute the emptier side fades out. Then two new songs. Walk, don't run, across the floor.

modalities.name: Hands Above the Circle
modalities.tagline: Lie in a ring, heads in, and dance with your arms overhead.
modalities.whatItIs: A gentle group session in which people lie on mats in a ring, heads toward the middle, and dance slowly with their arms and hands in the air above them to soft music, watching everyone's hands meet, echo and weave over the center. No one stands up, and there is no timer and no target, the opposite end of the scale from HIIT's timed, all-out bursts.
modalities.coreIdea: Dancing does not need a dance floor or a sweat to be shared, and lying down with only the arms moving keeps effort low while the sight of a circle of hands is meant to keep people connected. The low effort is meant to let company, not exercise, set the pace.
modalities.whatYouDo: Six to fourteen people lie on mats with cushions under their knees, and a host plays easy songs for about 45 minutes while people move their arms slowly, follow a neighbor's hand, or rest their arms and just watch. Between songs anyone may say what a song brings to mind, though no one is asked to, and the session ends with a few minutes of stillness before everyone rolls to one side and sits up slowly.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are tired, recovering or simply not interested in exercise and would still like to share music and movement with others. Anyone who cannot get down to the floor can join from a chair at the edge of the ring.
modalities.cautions: Get down to and up from the floor slowly, keep arm movements within an easy range for shoulders and necks, rest your arms whenever they tire, and let hands brush only when both people are happy with it. Songs can stir strong memories, so share only memories you already have and feel fine sharing, treat nothing a song stirs as evidence of what happened, never use the session to dig for forgotten events, and anyone can stop sharing or sit up and leave quietly at any time.
modalities.tweet: Not every dance needs you on your feet. Idea: lie in a ring on mats, heads in, and dance with only your arms to soft songs, watching all the hands weave above the middle. No timer, no sweat. Get down and up slowly, or join from a chair.

modalities.name: Charcoal Duets
modalities.tagline: Two people dance slowly on a big sheet, leaving one shared drawing.
modalities.whatItIs: A guided practice in which two people dance a slow, improvised duet on a large sheet of paper taped to the floor, each holding a stick of charcoal, so every move they make together leaves a mark. Afterwards they stand back and look at the drawing their duet made. Team sport pulls against opponents at speed in a crowd for a score; here there is one partner, a slow tempo, nothing to win, and the only record is a picture made by both.
modalities.coreIdea: Seeing a duet as a drawing shows how two people moved together: where they crowded each other, where one followed and where one held back. Making and reading that picture with a guide is meant to give a pair a gentle, concrete way to notice how they share space.
modalities.whatYouDo: A pair meets a dance teacher or dance movement therapist for three 60-minute sessions a few weeks apart, warms up, then dances slowly to calm music across a sheet about three meters square, sometimes standing and sometimes low on knees and hands, with charcoal in one hand, for two or three songs per drawing. After each drawing the pair stands back and, prompted by the guide's questions, says what they notice in it, and each session ends with one last duet on a fresh sheet that they keep.
modalities.whoItsFor: Friends, partners or relatives who would like a quiet, cooperative project that shows them something about how they move together. It may suit anyone who finds group sport too loud or competitive.
modalities.cautions: Tape the paper down on a clear, non-slip floor, use knee pads for low work, keep level changes easy on knees and backs, agree on any touch first, and use compressed charcoal in a ventilated room, since the dust can bother lungs and eyes. Warm up, check with a doctor first if you have heart, joint or balance problems and stop for pain, chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and the guide keeps the talk on what the drawing shows, never on blame.
modalities.tweet: A proposed practice for two: dance slowly together on a huge sheet of paper, each holding a stick of charcoal, then stand back and look at what your duet drew. Where you crowded, where you followed, where you held back. No score. Tape the paper down first.

modalities.name: Only the Finales
modalities.tagline: A sociable afternoon of dancing only the last minute of each song.
modalities.whatItIs: A host-led social afternoon in which the group stays on its feet through each song, swaying, clapping along and wandering about to chat, then dances only its last 60 to 90 seconds full out together, finishing on a shared final pose. Instead of one long, steady effort, usually alone, as in endurance training, the afternoon is a string of short, shared endings, with the pace set by the whole room.
modalities.coreIdea: A clear finish, reached together again and again, may give some of the satisfaction of completing something without anyone having to keep going hard for long. Easy movement and talk between the bursts are meant to make the afternoon about company first and effort second.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once a week for 90 minutes, 8 to 30 people meet in a community room with a host who teaches a few simple ending moves, such as a travelling step, a clap pattern and a final pose, and plays 20 to 25 songs that members have asked for. Through each song everyone sways, claps along and walks about chatting, then on the final chorus the room dances the host's ending full out and holds the pose for the last note, with the endings growing a little bigger as the afternoon goes on and chairs around the edge for anyone who wants a rest.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find long exercise sessions lonely or daunting and would rather move in short bursts with others. It may suit mixed-age groups and anyone who loves the big finish of a song.
modalities.cautions: Ninety minutes on your feet adds up, so wear supportive shoes, sit out any song you like, keep the endings simple, let anyone dance seated and ask before taking anyone's hands; anyone with heart, joint or balance problems should check with a doctor first, warm up with the host and stop for chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Members can say why they asked for a song or keep it to themselves, and any memory shared is one they already have and are happy to talk about; nothing a song stirs is treated as evidence of what happened, and the afternoon is never used to uncover forgotten events.
modalities.tweet: What if a dance afternoon were only finales? Everyone sways and chats through each song, then dances the last chorus full out together and holds the final pose. Gentle most of the time, big at the end. A new idea. Sit out any song, and warm up first.

modalities.name: Balloon Ballroom
modalities.tagline: Dance as lightly as possible while keeping balloons afloat together.
modalities.whatItIs: A playful group dance session where the aim is lightness: moving softly while keeping balloons and scarves floating in the air together, with nothing lifted and nothing counted, the opposite of strength training's heavy loads in strict sets. Losing a balloon is part of the fun.
modalities.coreIdea: Thinking of the body as light and the task as play, rather than as a load to overcome, may let effort feel easy and shared. Balloons give everyone a slow, floating target that invites soft, unhurried movement, and for some people an echo of childhood games.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a gentle warm-up, a facilitator plays bouncy music while 10 to 25 people move freely around a hall, tapping balloons upward with any part of the body and floating scarves to each other, adding balloons as the group finds its rhythm. Halfway through the group tries to keep every balloon up for a whole song, and the 50-minute session ends with everyone drifting slowly as the balloons settle.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel heavy, stiff or weighed down and want a light, silly way to move with others. It may also suit anyone who has only ever exercised to build muscle or lose weight and wants movement that asks for nothing.
modalities.cautions: Reaching and lunging for balloons can cause collisions and falls, so warm up gently, use a clear room and soft-soled shoes, walk rather than run, and use latex-free balloons in case of allergies. Anyone with heart, joint or balance problems should check with a doctor first or tap balloons from a chair, and everyone stops for pain, chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness.
modalities.tweet: What if exercise asked you to be light instead of strong? Suggested: 50 minutes of dancing to keep balloons and scarves afloat together, moving softly, losing them, laughing. Nothing lifted, nothing counted. Latex-free balloons and a clear floor.

modalities.name: Shared Screen Floor
modalities.tagline: Friends far apart dance live, treating a split screen as one floor.
modalities.whatItIs: A self-run weekly video call for friends who live apart, in which two to four households dance live side by side on a split screen and treat the edges of their boxes as one shared floor: tossing an imagined ball from box to box, ducking as it flies past, meeting hands at the borders and answering each other's moves as they happen. Everything animal-assisted therapy depends on, a trained team, a special setting and a calm, non-human partner, is absent: just ordinary kitchens and living rooms, friends you already know, a lot of laughing and no professional at all.
modalities.coreIdea: Pretending the screen is one room asks everyone to watch the others closely and answer them the moment they move, which may turn a call into something playful and physical. Doing it every week is meant to keep a friendship lively between real visits.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once a week, two to six friends in two to four homes join a 40-minute call with everyone shown side by side, clear a space, warm up together to one song and then take turns calling a game for each song, such as passing the imagined ball along the row, meeting hands at the box edges or leaning together so the row ripples like one long wave. The call ends with one song danced however each person likes and a few minutes of chat.
modalities.whoItsFor: Friends who live far apart and want a lively way to spend time together between visits. It may suit people who like dancing at home but miss having someone to dance with.
modalities.cautions: Home dancing means hard floors, furniture and corners, and watching a screen while you move makes trips more likely, so clear a space, set the screen at eye level, wear proper shoes, warm up, check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems and stop for chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Nobody records the call unless everyone agrees, and nobody owes attendance in a busy week.
modalities.tweet: Friends far apart, one shared floor: a new idea for a weekly video call where you dance side by side, treat the screen edges as one room, toss an imagined ball from box to box and meet hands at the borders. Clear the furniture first.

modalities.name: Where the Beam Lands
modalities.tagline: In a dim hall, whoever the torch lights up dances big.
modalities.whatItIs: A playful group dance in a dimly lit hall where one person holds a strong torch and sweeps its beam slowly across the floor: anyone it lands on dances big, fast and wild, and everyone in shadow keeps moving small and soft until the light finds them. The torch changes hands every song, so nobody knows where the energy will flare next.
modalities.coreIdea: Energy is spent in sudden, unpredictable bursts that pass around a room full of people, the reverse of qigong's one slow, set form for settling and gathering it, often alone. Not knowing when your turn will come is meant to keep everyone alert, laughing and ready to change in an instant.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a teacher-led warm-up with the lights up, 12 to 30 people dance for about 45 minutes to upbeat music with the main lights dimmed but never off, while the torch holder walks the edge of the room keeping the beam low, at chest height or below. Anyone can step out of the beam to rest, and the session ends with the lights back up and one slow song for everyone.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel stuck in routine or flat and want a lively, surprising way to move with others. It may suit those who enjoy a moment in the light in small doses, as well as those who prefer the dim corners.
modalities.cautions: Keep a dim light on so nobody trips, clear the floor, never shine the beam at faces or eyes, use a steady beam with no flashing, and tell people with light sensitivity or a history of seizures in advance. Warm up, keep jumps optional, check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems and stop for pain, chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness.
modalities.tweet: Dim the lights and give one dancer a torch. Anyone the beam lands on dances big and wild; everyone in shadow keeps it small until the light finds them. New holder every song. An experimental game. Keep the beam low and away from faces.

modalities.name: All Four Parts
modalities.tagline: Four dancers, four different parts, swapped every week.
modalities.whatItIs: A teacher-led practice in which a fixed crew of four learns a short, demanding quartet where each dancer has a different part at the same moment: one stays low near the floor, one travels around the others, one turns on the spot and one takes the big jumps or a no-jump version. Every week each dancer moves on to the next part, so over a month everyone dances every place in the piece. In place of the easy talk with many people that makes up socializing, it offers a structured, physical way to know three people well, through the exact demands of where each of them stands.
modalities.coreIdea: Dancing the part a friend danced last week is meant to show you, in your own legs and lungs, what their place in the group asks of them. Knowing a small crew from the inside of its parts is meant to build a practical respect that grows out of shared work rather than chat.
modalities.whatYouDo: The crew meets a teacher once a week for 75 minutes in a studio or hall: after a warm-up, the teacher coaches each dancer in the part they are taking over, the four parts are fitted back together slowly, and the quartet is then run five or six times to lively music. Each session ends with every dancer saying in a sentence or two what their new part asked of them, and after four weeks a final session runs the quartet four times, once in each arrangement.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find mingling tiring but would like to know a few others well through something hard and shared. It may suit friends, flatmates or colleagues who enjoy precise, structured movement.
modalities.cautions: Each part has its own strain, so the teacher offers a gentler version of every part, jumps stay optional, the four keep an arm's length apart on a clear, non-slip floor and everyone warms up first. Check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems, stop at once for chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and agree on any touch before it happens.
modalities.tweet: Proposed: four friends learn a short, lively dance in which each has a different part (low, travelling, turning, jumping), then swap parts every week until all four have danced every place. You learn what each spot asks of a friend. Warm up, jumps optional.

modalities.name: Taped Floor Patterns
modalities.tagline: Indoor group dances that trace exact paths across a taped floor.
modalities.whatItIs: A teacher-led indoor dance class where the floor is marked with taped lines, circles and grids, and every dance follows exact paths across them. It reverses the free wandering of a nature walk through open, living terrain: the room is built, the space itself is designed and every route is planned. Dancers learn to move as shapes on a map.
modalities.coreIdea: A clearly mapped space removes the question of where to go, and tracing exact paths with others turns the group into a visible, changing pattern. The precision is meant to be absorbing and energizing rather than calming.
modalities.whatYouDo: Before class the teacher tapes a pattern onto a hall floor, and after a warm-up 10 to 24 people learn a lively routine that sends them along the lines in groups, crossing, circling and meeting at marked points. Each week brings a new floor pattern, and in the last session students design one themselves and teach it to the group.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like order, puzzles and clear rules, or who feel lost in open, unstructured settings. It may also suit those who want lively exercise indoors whatever the weather.
modalities.cautions: Tape edges can lift and trip people, and crossing paths at speed risks collisions, so use flat, well-stuck floor tape, keep speeds moderate and warm up first. Check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems, and stop for pain, chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness.
modalities.tweet: Tape lines, circles and a grid onto a hall floor, then dance the routes together, crossing and meeting at marked points like a living diagram. An untested idea that pairs order with energy, indoors in any weather. Mind the tape edges.

modalities.name: Dance the Lyrics Out
modalities.tagline: Sing along loudly and dance out what the words say.
modalities.whatItIs: A teacher-led group class in which everyone sings along to well-known songs and dances out the lyrics, from a literal 'reach for the sky' to little scenes made up in small groups. Plain, quiet sensation, the heart of sensory mindfulness, gives way to words, stories and voices shared out loud with a room full of people, while the body still does most of the work.
modalities.coreIdea: Turning words into movement, and singing while you do it, gives meaning a loud, physical outlet and makes everyone part of one noisy chorus. The playfulness is meant to lift energy and loosen self-consciousness.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a warm-up, the teacher plays a song and shows a few literal moves for the chorus, then small groups of four to six invent moves for a verse and teach them to the room. Over 75 minutes the class builds three or four songs this way and ends by singing and dancing them all through at full volume.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who sing in the car and dance in the kitchen but would never do either in front of others on their own. It may also suit groups who want an exuberant, low-skill way to dance together.
modalities.cautions: Singing while dancing hard is demanding, so warm up, take breaks, check with a doctor first if you have heart, lung or joint problems, agree before any touch in a group scene and stop at once for chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Songs can bring up memories, so share only what you already remember and feel fine sharing, treat nothing a song stirs as evidence of what happened, never use the class to dig for forgotten events, and choose songs whose words nobody in the group finds hurtful.
modalities.tweet: Ever sung along so hard you started acting out the words? Draft idea: a dance class built on exactly that. Groups invent moves for each line of a well-known song, then the whole room sings and dances it through. Warm up, and take breathers.

modalities.name: Window Tempo Dancing
modalities.tagline: Dance to the rhythms of a busy street instead of music.
modalities.whatItIs: A group dance practice done without music, in front of a large window onto a busy street or in an open public spot, where each round takes its tempo from something you can see: passing cars, people walking, pigeons, trees in the wind. Rhythm, which music therapy reaches through sound, listening and playing, has to be found here with the eyes, in the world outside. Each dancer may find a different beat in the same scene.
modalities.coreIdea: The everyday world is full of rhythms that usually go unnoticed, and dancing to them is meant to turn a familiar view into something lively and shared. Because nobody supplies a beat, each person has to find their own in what they see.
modalities.whatYouDo: A teacher warms up 6 to 20 people, then gives each round a source, such as cars, footsteps, a flag or the branches of a tree, and everyone dances to its rhythm for three or four minutes. Between rounds dancers show each other the beat they found, and the 50-minute session ends with everyone choosing their own source and dancing to it at once.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find loud music overwhelming, or who are curious what rhythm looks like when you cannot hear it. It may suit groups that mix deaf and hearing dancers, since nobody relies on sound.
modalities.cautions: Watching the world outside rather than the floor can lead to trips and bumps, so use a clear, even floor, keep good spacing and warm up first; outdoors, stay well back from roads and out of people's way. Check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems, and stop for chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness.
modalities.tweet: Imagine dancing to a city street instead of a song: one round to passing cars, one to people's footsteps, one to a tree in the wind. No music at all, just rhythm found with your eyes. A new idea, untested. Clear floor, and stay well back from the road.
